newsitem.title: CANADA: Ranger sets sights on Angola deep waters.
newsitem.headline: Ranger sets sights on Angola deep waters.

text.p: Ranger Oil Ltd expects Angola to play a much bigger role in its operations in the next few years and it has designs on the oil region's ultra-deep waters, Ranger Chief Operating Officer Phil Irwin said.

Ranger sees Angola, where the company currently operates Block 4 on the coastal shelf, eventually making up 25 to 30 percent of its operations portfolio, with the North Sea remaining its "crown jewel," Irwin said.

"Five years out, I would certainly hope that Ranger is heading a consortium that is producing 100,000 barrels of oil a day, with Ranger having somewhere between 30 and 40 percent of that," he said in an interview this week.

Offshore Angola is the site of busy exploration by most of the world's major oil companies. Industry players have speculated that some recently discovered fields could harbor several billions of barrels of oil, although the operators remained tight-lipped on their reserve estimates.
In the areas south and west of the Congo River, the main geological play is the Pinda formation, but recent finds have been made in the Tertiary, which lies above it, Irwin said.

Discoveries have also grown in size in the relatively young exploration region as players plumbed the deeper waters. Bidding on blocks sitting in depths of about 2,000 metres offshore Angola was expected to start after the current round for Blocks 23, 24 and 25 ends in September or October.

Ranger intends to participate in what was expected to be aggressive bidding for the ultra-deep plays, whose exploration has been made easier with recent strides in deep drilling technology developed in the Gulf of Mexico and North Sea.
Huge oil discoveries have been widely rumored on two deep offshore Angola areas, Block 14 and Block 17.
France's Elf Aquitaine discovered the Girassol field in 1,300 feet of water on Block 17 in April 1996.
Analysts and industry players have speculated that Girassol's recoverable reserves could be between one billon and 3.5 billion barrels of oil.
Elf's partners on Block 17 include Exxon Corp, British Petroleum Co Plc, Den Norske Stats Oljeselskap (Statoil), Norsk Hydro and Fina Inc.
Block 14 is the site of the 14-2X discovery drilled in April by operator Chevron Corp.
Although Chevron said it was too early to estimate reserves indicated by the discovery, numerous industry watchers have speculated commercial reserves to be one billion to 1.5 billion barrrels.
Chevron's partners include Angola state oil company SONANGOL, Agip Angola, Total Angola and Petrogal Petroleos de Portugal.

Ranger was recently granted Angola government approval as operator to develop the comparatively small Kiame field on its 1.2 million acre Block 4, which has reserves estimated at eight million barrels. It is expected to start producing in the second quarter of 1998, reaching 7,000 barrels a day.

Another Ranger discovery made at the western tip of the block last year, 4/31-1-3, flowed at 6,500 barrels a day from the Tertiary. Irwin said the well was drilled without the benefit of 3D seismic, which has since been shot in the area.

"We've mapped some sand channels around there that give us confidence that we'll be able to parley that into a 100 million barrel oil field," he said. "Now, our business is based on confidense and optimism, but all that we can see is very positive."
